source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?
finding: Self-repair (model debugs its own code) often gives only small gains once compute cost is counted; it can lose to just drawing more fresh samples.
numbers: GPT-4 on APPS: 10 initial samples plus 1 repair each = 1.05x pass rate of pass@20; 2 initial samples plus 10 repairs each = 0.97x of pass@22.
limits: Only HumanEval and APPS, Python. Compute-matched comparison is the key design point.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a repair loop beats more independent attempts at equal budget. Spend budget on diverse first hypotheses (matches S3).

source: Olausson et al. (2024) human feedback experiment
finding: The bottleneck of repair is the quality of the diagnosis (the feedback). Human expert explanations of the bug raise GPT-4 repair success a lot.
numbers: Repair success, GPT-4 feedback vs human feedback: introductory 42.64% vs 62.21%; interview 19.33% vs 45.67%; competition 3.67% vs 14.67%; overall 33.30% vs 52.60%. 16 participants, 40 failing programs, 2 feedbacks each, 25 repairs per feedback.
limits: Small human study (16 people, about 1 hour each). Gap grows with task difficulty.
agent_relevance: Fault localisation and explanation is the weak step, not the patch. Put effort and a stronger check on the diagnosis stage.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Self-correction without an outside signal lowers accuracy. Earlier gains came from using oracle labels to decide when to stop.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 after round 1 and 41.8 after round 2. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0. With oracle labels GPT-3.5 GSM8K rises 75.9 to 95.5; HotpotQA 26.0 to 49.0 (GPT-3.5) and 29.0 to 59.0 (GPT-4).
limits: Intrinsic self-correction on reasoning QA, not tool-using fault finding. On GSM8K the model kept its answer 74.7% of the time; changes went more often from right to wrong.
agent_relevance: A reflection step with no real test (S7) hurts. Only revise when a genuine external check returns a signal.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey
finding: Survey of self-correction work: no prior work shows success with feedback from prompted LLMs in general tasks; success needs reliable external feedback or large-scale fine-tuning.
numbers: Three conclusions: (1) no success with prompted-LLM feedback in general tasks; (2) works where reliable external tools exist; (3) fine-tuning at scale enables it.
limits: I read the abstract, introduction and section 5 text. Warns that many positive results use unfair oracle or external information.
agent_relevance: Matches Huang 2024. For every internal test ask whether feedback is external or only the model's own opinion.

source: Chen et al. (2025) AIOpsLab
finding: LLM agents were tested on injected faults in microservice clouds across four tasks. Accuracy falls from detecting to locating to root cause to fixing.
numbers: Overall accuracy: GPT-4-w-shell 49.15%, GPT-3.5-w-shell 15.25%, ReAct 55.93%, FLASH 59.32%. Root cause task: GPT-4 40.90%, GPT-3.5 9.09%, ReAct 45.45%, FLASH 36.36%. Mitigation: GPT-4 27.27%, GPT-3.5 0%, FLASH 36.36%.
limits: pdftotext garbled the tables; the overall column mapping follows the paper text (FLASH 59.32%, GPT-3.5 15.25%). Small problem set (13 detection, 11 RCA problems).
agent_relevance: Root-cause naming is hard even when detection is easy. Expect later stages to be the weak ones.

source: Chen et al. (2025) AIOpsLab: step limit analysis
finding: More steps stop helping after about 5 steps; environment feedback alone saturates fast on ops faults.
numbers: FLASH reached 59.32% at the highest step limit; a limit above 5 did not improve the other agents but raised token use. Detection: GPT-3.5 23.07%, GPT-4 69.23%, ReAct 76.92%, only FLASH answered all detection problems right.
limits: Authors contrast with code tasks where linters and tests keep helping.
agent_relevance: Longer loops are not the fix. Add better task decomposition and intermediate checks, as the authors suggest.

source: Jha et al. (2025) ITBench
finding: Frontier agents solve few real SRE incident scenarios; success drops sharply with scenario complexity.
numbers: Resolved 13.8% of SRE, 25.2% of CISO, 0% of FinOps scenarios (94 scenarios). Diagnosis pass@1 for gpt-4o: easy 36.00, medium 7.73, hard 5.00. Repair pass@1: easy 21.00, medium 12.27, hard 0.00. No agent fixed any of five hard scenarios.
limits: Complexity model uses propagation chain length, resolution steps, technology diversity. Appendix tables cover 42 SRE scenarios with repeated runs.
agent_relevance: Complexity (long causal chain, many technologies) is the main difficulty axis, matching the complexity framing of this subfield.

source: Jha et al. (2025) ITBench: diagnosis and repair are decoupled
finding: Agents sometimes repair with a wrong root-cause belief, and sometimes diagnose well but cannot repair. Results vary between repeated runs.
numbers: Scenario 15: llama-3.3-70b named 'memory limit' (true cause HTTP request corruption) yet scaled replicas and cleared the alert. Scenario 13 (easy): no agent repaired it, but gpt-4o had about 80% diagnosis pass@1. Some scenarios succeeded in only 1 of 10 runs.
limits: Descriptive case analysis, not a controlled test.
agent_relevance: Score diagnosis and repair separately. A cleared alert is not proof the cause was found.

source: Nori et al. (2025) Sequential Diagnosis with Language Models
finding: On 304 NEJM clinicopathological cases run as step by step diagnosis, a structured panel of prompted model roles beat doctors and the same model without structure.
numbers: Generalist physicians (median 12 years) 20% accuracy at $2,963 per case. GPT-4o 49.3% at $2,745. o3 78.6% at $7,850. MAI-DxO with o3: 79.9% at $2,397; 81.9% at $4,735 (no budget); 85.5% at $7,184 with ensembling.
limits: Physicians could not use search, books or colleagues; generalists only; no healthy cases so no false-positive rate. Cases are curated and hard.
agent_relevance: Hypothesis tracking, an adversarial challenger and a cost steward add accuracy and cut cost together (S3, S7).

source: Nori et al. (2025) failure analysis of the off-the-shelf model
finding: Authors found the plain model anchored on first impressions and ordered tests that were reasonable rather than ones that cut uncertainty most per dollar.
numbers: The hypothesis-tracking role (Dr. Hypothesis) and adversarial role (Dr. Challenger) led the orchestrator to seek disconfirming evidence and switch paths on cases where it disagreed with plain o3. Example: o3 fixated on antibiotic toxicity and ordered costly imaging for a hand-sanitiser ingestion.
limits: Qualitative inspection of disagreement cases; no single-role ablation in the text I read.
agent_relevance: Maps to anti-anchoring and discriminating-test operators. Test value per cost is a missing operator in plain prompting.

source: Liu et al. (2024) DebugBench
finding: Debugging difficulty rises with bug type; logic and multi-bug faults are hardest.
numbers: 4,253 instances in C++, Java, Python. GPT-4 pass rate: missing colons 93.6, undefined methods 78.5, condition error 73.1, variable error 63.1, double bugs 70.7, triple 58.9, quadruple 55.9. Human (12 attempts per type): syntax 11-12 of 12, triple bugs 9/12, quadruple 8/12.
limits: Bugs were implanted by GPT-4 into LeetCode code, not real bugs. Human sample small (about 12 per type). Zero-shot only.
agent_relevance: Number of simultaneous faults is a clear complexity driver; plan for interacting faults, not one.

source: Liu et al. (2024) DebugBench runtime feedback
finding: Runtime messages help locate syntax and reference bugs but are often too low-level for logic bugs and may disrupt the fix.
numbers: Figure 4 for gpt-4-0613: clear gain from traceback on syntax and reference errors, little or negative effect on logic errors (exact bar values not read from the text).
limits: I read the text, not the plotted bar values.
agent_relevance: A test result must be at the right level of abstraction to count as evidence. Summarise a trace as a claim about the hypothesis.

source: Roy et al. (2024) Exploring LLM-based Agents for Root Cause Analysis
finding: A ReAct agent with retrieval tools matched strong baselines on correctness but made far fewer false statements. Adding discussion comments did not help.
numbers: Manual labels on 97 test incidents: retrieval baseline (k=10) and CoT 39% correct, ReAct 35%. Hallucination in correct answers: retrieval 26% (10/38), CoT and ReAct under 1%. Hallucination in incorrect answers: retrieval 49% (29/59), CoT 18% (11/59), ReAct 6% (4/63). 66% of ReAct errors were 'insufficient information'.
limits: Only general tools in the main test; lexical metric differences within noise (C-BLEU). Small labelled sample.
agent_relevance: Tool-using hypothesis testing reduces made-up causes and gives honest 'not enough evidence'. Value is trust, not raw hit rate.

source: Ahmed et al. (2023) Recommending Root-Cause and Mitigation Steps for Cloud Incidents using LLMs
finding: Field study at Microsoft: 44,340 incidents from 1,759 services. Incident owners rated model suggestions as useful on average.
numbers: Human check by 25 incident owners on 50 recent incidents. Best-of-OpenAI-options mean correctness and readability 3.52 to 4.64 of 5; single-model correctness 2.28 to 3.16; over 70% of owners gave 3 or more. Encoder-decoder baselines were rated lower and more generic.
limits: Fine-tuned GPT-3.x, no tools, past incident text only; owners picked the best of six options so scores are best-case. Older models.
agent_relevance: Generic answers pass lexical metrics but fail human tests; check specificity. Expert best-of-several selection inflates scores.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts
finding: Planning questions by expected information gain raises success in 20 Questions, medical diagnosis and a car or laptop troubleshooting dialogue task.
numbers: Average +38.1% success over direct prompting across 5 datasets and 5 LLMs. Troubleshooting (FloDial, up to 20 turns): GPT-4 43.7% to 67.3% success, mean questions 7.8. Open-ended diagnosis with GPT-4 reached 88.0%.
limits: Answers simulated by GPT-4; benchmarks simplified (fixed candidate set); authors say real open-ended cases are harder.
agent_relevance: Question choice by information gain is a concrete testable operator for the discriminating-test step.

source: Laban et al. (2025) LLMs Get Lost In Multi-Turn Conversation
finding: When facts arrive over several turns, all tested models do worse than when given everything at once. Main causes are unreliability and early commitment.
numbers: Average drop 39% over six generation tasks and 200,000+ simulated conversations; aptitude loss about 15%, unreliability up 112%.
quote: when LLMs take a wrong turn in a conversation, they get lost and do not recover
limits: Simulated users; generation tasks (code, SQL, math, summaries), not diagnosis.
agent_relevance: Troubleshooting is a multi-turn evidence game, so premature closure is the expected failure. Do not commit before key evidence; restart from scratch if the early guess fails.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?
finding: Failure taxonomy over 1,600+ traces from 7 multi-agent frameworks: 14 modes in 3 groups, including premature termination and missing or wrong verification.
numbers: Failure rate 41% to 86.7% across 7 open-source systems. Inter-annotator kappa 0.88 on 150 traces. Task verification family: premature termination, no or incomplete verification, incorrect verification.
limits: I read the abstract and taxonomy listing, not each per-mode share. Not specific to troubleshooting.
agent_relevance: Verification and stopping are separate failure classes; build a verifier and a stop rule instead of trusting agent talk.

source: Sabuncu et al. (ASEE) interview and think-aloud study of expert troubleshooting
finding: Known here only from the project SUBFIELDS file: 18 engineers with over 10 years' experience interviewed; two think-aloud cases compared; five manifolds proposed. Paper not opened.
numbers: N=18 interviews; 2 think-aloud cases; preliminary, no statistics.
limits: Secondhand. One expert sought system understanding first; a PhD student only as needed for root-cause search.
agent_relevance: Experts alternate divergent and convergent work; an agent plan should allow that rather than a linear script.

source: Hu and Ash (2026) LLM help for circuit debugging
finding: Known only from SUBFIELDS: LLMs gave sensible suggestions but struggled with images and sounded overconfident. Not opened.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Secondhand.
agent_relevance: Overconfidence in hardware diagnosis matches guardrail G10.

source: Daly, Anand, Abel: Industry Perspectives on Mechanical Engineering Troubleshooting (ASEE)
finding: Found in the Crossref index as a related ASEE paper. Full text blocked (403). Not read.
numbers: None.
limits: Listed only to mark a gap.
agent_relevance: Another place to look for expert interview models of troubleshooting.

source: Gugerty (2007) Cognitive components of troubleshooting strategies
finding: Found through Crossref, behind a paywall. Not read. Needed for human strategy evidence.
numbers: None.
limits: Listed to mark a gap in human-side evidence.
agent_relevance: If obtained, would give measured human strategy effects.

source: Chen et al. (2025) AIOpsLab: LLM agents vs classic AIOps tools
finding: All LLM agents beat the older non-LLM AIOps tools on detection and localisation.
numbers: Localisation Acc@1: GPT-4 61.54%, ReAct 53.85%, FLASH 46.15% vs PDiagnose 15.38% and RMLAD 7.69%. Detection: MKSMC 15.38% (as read).
limits: Table text partly garbled; numbers for non-LLM tools as read.
agent_relevance: Language reasoning over logs and metrics adds real diagnostic power over statistical detectors.

source: Roy et al. (2024) RCA agents: discussions did not help
finding: Adding the human discussion comments from incident reports as extra input did not significantly improve root-cause predictions.
numbers: Stated in the abstract: 'surprisingly does not yield significant performance improvements'.
limits: Abstract-level; I did not extract per-metric deltas.
agent_relevance: More context is not automatically better evidence; unvetted chatter can add noise.

source: Ahmed et al. (2023) machine vs human detected incidents
finding: Fine-tuned models did a little better on machine-detected than human-detected incidents. Gains were largest on Top1 METEOR.
numbers: Davinci-002 Top1 METEOR 9.41 (machine detected) vs 7.65 (human detected), a 23.01% gain; BLEU-4 Top1 7.18 vs 6.56; 592 test incidents.
limits: Lexical metrics only for this table.
agent_relevance: Structured, machine-generated symptoms are easier to diagnose than free-form human reports; clean the input (S1).

source: Huang et al. (2024) GPT-4 retains answers; GPT-3.5 flips them
finding: Stronger models are more likely to keep their first answer after a self-correction prompt, and weaker ones flip right answers to wrong ones.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA fell from 75.8 to 38.1 (round 1); GPT-4 and GPT-4-Turbo mostly retained their initial answers, possibly from higher confidence.
limits: Reasoning QA benchmarks; not diagnosis.
agent_relevance: Re-checking can add risk. A diagnosis already supported by a test should be locked, not reopened by a vague prompt.
